Ever watched a hacking sequence in a movie and thought it looked equal parts ridiculous and cool? Hacknet leans into that fantasy while bringing the learning curve down to something genuinely manageable. Even a passing familiarity with command line will make this click, and if you have none at all, the in-game guidance and Steam's community resources fill in the gaps. Don't let the aesthetic intimidate you — it's far more approachable than it looks, and more fun and challenging than I expected.

I originally attempted this back in 2019 and bounced off it. Coming back now and having forgotten nearly everything I knew turned out to be a blessing. This was my first real dive into a command-line driven game, and while there is a GUI available for when you blank on specific commands or syntax, you'll spend most of your time in the terminal. The game gives you everything you need — but only if you actually read and retain the instructions when they appear. I found myself referencing help commands repeatedly and still making mistakes, which is entirely on me rather than the game. It's patient with you, as long as you're patient with it.

Progress doesn't always feel linear, which threw me at first, but it's part of the appeal. Every device you breach opens up a small world of its own — old chat rooms, private email exchanges between people living secret lives, someone just trying to organize a D&D session. The incidental storytelling is often genuinely funny, and the referenced media scattered throughout is a welcome discovery. The broader narrative — working your way up through hacker organizations, breaching servers to obtain, remove, or alter data — takes roughly three quarters of the runtime to fully reveal itself, but what surrounds it keeps things moving.

The soundtrack deserves particular attention. Sourced through Boss Battle Records across a range of artists — Carpenter Brut being the most familiar name — it's superb from start to finish. What makes it exceptional for a 2015 release is how dynamically it shifts and adapts based on what's happening in-game. I've already added it to regular rotation well after finishing.

At $10 full price and as low as $1.50 on sale, there's genuinely nothing to debate. Bundle it if you can, buy it regardless if you can't. Don't let the look of it put you off. 88/100

There is a game from the PS2/GameCube era that I have a fond memory of, called Enter the Matrix. It was nothing special, clunky controls and a relatively tame story that tied into the movie series, but it had one unique minigame you could play around in that also worked as a way to enable cheats in the main game.

The minigame was a hacking simulator (of sorts) in relation to the Matrix universe. I distinctly remember it being rudimentary, since you didn't have a keyboard to navigate the system and had to rely on your controller's joystick, but it presented a unique challenge that allowed you to dig up some unique easter eggs.

The reason I have a fond memory of this particular minigame is because it gave you zero information to work with, instead, it presented a few items of interest and if you started to dig you would find a common thread leading you to this one inconsequential easter egg.

I don't even remember the easter egg; I believe it was a prerecorded soundbite from Neo. Nevertheless, what I remember is the minigame never held your hand, only showing you how to navigate the system and your own curiosity leading the way.

This game recaptured that feeling. I had no idea what to expect but what I discovered is a game that very minimally holds your hand and forces you to utilize the tools at your disposal to solve a mystery. If you allowed your curiosity to guide you, then you will eventually uncover the truth.

This is a fantastic game hiding in the shadows, so to speak. I thoroughly enjoyed the authentic feel of the overworld and the objective-less system, instead giving you instructions (sometime vague) on how to accomplish your mission.

This game also presented a few unique challenges I wasn't even expecting. I think it's safe to say there are three unique moments where you can outright fail if you're slow enough, but all equally present an opportunity to fix your mistakes. If you're quick enough, you can avoid the mistakes in their entirety, which is deeply rewarding in and of itself.

Overall, give this game a shot if you want a near-authentic hacking experience without having to worry about utilizing known computer languages.

I bought this game 6 years ago, and today I finally achieved 100% completion.
Looking back, the journey was entirely worth it. Back then, I needed to improve my English and analytical skills to fully grasp everything, but coming back to finish it has been one of the most rewarding gaming experiences I've ever had.
Hacknet is a fantastic game. It completely sucks you into its digital world, creating an immersive, lovely feeling that few other games can replicate. 
What truly sets it apart are the tiny, hidden details scattered throughout the systems... discovering them makes the world feel incredibly alive and real.
Very few games can make me feel this genuinely happy and satisfied while playing, but Hacknet is absolutely one of them.

 If you love puzzles, deep atmosphere, and a game that challenges you a little bit, buy this immediately.

Rating: 10/10

Not super accurate to real life hacking, as the game does trivialize hacking with a few made up tools, especially with SSHcrack, as in real life secure shell is an incredibly secure protocol for remote terminal access, and real life hacking will tend to come down to finding exploits in propritary protocols, or even as far as running exploit chains that are very particular. All this to say, you can learn some basic linux shell commands through this game such as working through filesystems, but beyond that most things are very oversimplified, so don't play with the expectation that you will gain any true pentesting skills. But it can be fun for a couple of hours here and there if you're in the mood for a gmae like this.

A riveting game about digitally going where you shouldn't be, seeing things you shouldn't see, and breaking things some would leave be. Explore the world through a basic interface and command window, worming your way through ports, proxies, and firewalls while avoiding detection by tracers and the occasional counter-hacker. Engage with a high-stakes story in both the base game and the DLC which will leave you wondering whether you made the right choices.

In short, a very fun and thoughtful game.

Do note you will need to read fast, type fast, and concentrate to get through some of the later barriers, especially in the DLC. While the game is largely text-based, that text often requires fast input. Mouse, keyboard, and keypad highly recommended.
